title: The Trades Labor Shortage and What It Means for Marketing
content:
###  **A Constraint That Changes the Question** 

Industry observers including ServiceTitan have noted a persistent pattern: as older generations retire from the trades, home service companies are finding it difficult to attract newer generations into these careers. 

Meanwhile the market keeps growing. The United States home services sector is above $600 billion and expanding at a mid-to-high single digit rate annually. 

More demand, fewer people to serve it. 

###  **What This Does to Marketing Strategy** 

When a company can take every job it can find, more leads are unambiguously better. When crew capacity is the limiting factor, that stops being true. 

A company that cannot staff more work does not benefit from a larger pile of unqualified leads. It benefits from better ones — higher value jobs, closer together, with less time lost to estimates that were never going to convert. 

###  **Why Sorted Leads Matter More Under Capacity Constraints** 

With limited crew hours, where those hours go becomes the central decision. Time spent driving to an estimate for a homeowner who was not serious is time that cannot be recovered. 

This is the practical case for leads that arrive qualified and sorted by timing rather than volume. A shorter list of homeowners who are ready is worth more than a longer list requiring the same sales hours to sift. 

###  **Geographic Concentration Becomes More Valuable** 

The same logic applies to territory. Jobs clustered in a few neighborhoods consume fewer crew hours in transit than the same number scattered across a region. 

When labor is the scarce resource, drive time is a direct cost against capacity. 

###  **The Reframe** 

In a market constrained by people rather than demand, the useful marketing question is no longer how to generate more leads. It is how to make sure the hours a company does have go toward the work most worth doing.
